transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I suppose I'm here because... well, it's been getting really difficult at work lately. I'm an artist, you see, and a lot of my work involves explaining my process, whether that's writing artist statements for galleries, or sending notes to clients, or even just talking in meetings with curators and collaborators. And lately, it's like... I'll start trying to explain the texture of a piece, you know, how the impasto catches the light, and then suddenly I'm talking about the budget for the exhibition, and then somehow that connects to these secret meanings I've been embedding in the color choices, and... and I know it all makes sense to me in the moment, the connections are so clear, but people keep stopping me. They look at me with these confused expressions and they tell me they can't follow what I'm trying to explain. It's incredibly frustrating because the vision is right there in my head, but by the time it gets out onto paper or out of my mouth, it's just this tangle that no one else can unravel. My last client actually asked if I had sent the wrong email because it jumped around so much, and that's when I thought maybe I should come talk to someone about it.
When you're experiencing these thoughts that jump around so much, do you notice any changes in your mood — like feeling unusually high, overly irritable, or down and depressed at the same time?

Oh, definitely. It's... well, it's actually really intense when it happens. For these long stretches, I just feel completely lit up from the inside out. It's like I have this boundless energy, and I feel almost unstoppable. I'll be in my studio, maybe it's the middle of the night, and every single idea that pops into my head just feels absolutely brilliant. I'll be mixing paints or sketching out a new installation, and I'm just thinking, "This is it, this is the piece that changes everything," and I just keep going and going because the inspiration is so incredibly strong and my mind is moving so fast. I just feel so fantastic. 

But then... the flip side of that—and this is what really causes problems, especially when I'm working with other people—is the irritability. I'll be in this amazing groove, feeling like a total visionary, and then a collaborator or a curator will make just one tiny, insignificant comment. Maybe they ask a simple question about a timeline, or they just don't immediately understand the concept I'm pitching, and I just... I snap. 

And I mean, I snap in a way that feels so much bigger than the situation actually calls for. I'll feel this sudden rush of anger, like they're trying to sabotage my entire artistic vision, and I'll just lash out at them. I've sent some really harsh emails over things that, looking back, were just standard feedback or a minor misunderstanding. It's like my fuse is completely nonexistent during those periods. I'm either on top of the world, completely untouchable and brilliant, or I'm biting someone's head off over absolutely nothing.

Have there been times when your mood and energy were so high that it significantly affected your ability to function normally — maybe you didn’t sleep for days, became so hyper-focused on your work that you ignored other responsibilities, or others noticed that your behavior was unusually erratic or extreme?

Oh, absolutely, it's just... it's like a floodgate opens and suddenly there aren't enough hours in the day, or I guess it feels more like I don't even need the hours to exist normally. When I get into that state, sleep just feels like this completely unnecessary, almost offensive interruption, you know? Like, why would I close my eyes when there is so much to do and the ideas are just pouring out of me at lightspeed? It affects absolutely everything. 

I’ll just suddenly, out of nowhere, decide to take on three massive exhibition proposals all at once, which is completely absurd because normally even one takes weeks of careful planning and drafting. But I'll be working on those, and then right in the middle of typing, I'll look around and decide the spatial flow in my workspace is completely blocking my creative aura, so I'll just drop the proposals and completely reorganize the entire studio. I mean dragging heavy drafting tables across the room by myself, sorting hundreds of tubes of paint by color family and opacity at two in the morning, putting up new shelving... it's exhausting just thinking about it now, but at the time I feel like I have the strength of ten people. 

And then, instead of resting after all that heavy lifting, I'll just sit down and sketch all night long. I'll fill up sketchbook after sketchbook until my hand is literally cramping and covered in graphite, but I just can't stop the momentum. By the time the sun comes up, I'm already on my laptop firing off these incredibly intense, urgent emails to curators and gallery directors—people I haven't even spoken to in months—pitching these massive, sprawling installations. And the craziest part is, before they even have a chance to reply, before I even have a dime of funding secured or a contract signed, I'm already pulling out my most expensive supplies and starting to cut materials for pieces I haven't even budgeted yet. I ruined about four hundred dollars worth of raw linen just last month because I started hacking into it with my shears, totally convinced I was constructing a masterpiece, without measuring a single thing or thinking about how I was going to pay my rent that week. It's just this absolute, unstoppable frenzy of doing, doing, doing, and I just can't seem to turn the motor off, no matter what else I'm actually supposed to be taking care of in my real life.
